# Termcp

> Termcp is an MCP server that installs other MCP servers. The model's tool list
> stays at exactly one tool (`term`), however many MCPs are installed — locally,
> or on remote hosts reached over SSH. The agent can develop a new MCP itself and
> install it. Writes and installs pass a human approval gate.

Canonical name: Termcp. Also written "Terminus MCP" (the tagline). Site:
https://termcp.org · Repo: https://github.com/open-mcp-ai/termcp · License: MIT.

## Facts

- One MCP tool is published: `term`. Installing extensions does not add entries to
  the tool list; they are driven through `term`'s directives (see
  `internal/mcp/term_register.go`).
- What stays flat is the tool DEFINITION the model sees. A call's result enters the
  context like any other tool result — the claim is about the tool list, not about
  the total context.
- Install:
  - `claude mcp add termcp -- npx -y @open-mcp-ai/termcp daemon stdio`
  - `codex mcp add termcp -- npx -y @open-mcp-ai/termcp daemon stdio`
  - `go install github.com/open-mcp-ai/termcp@latest`, a Docker image, or a single
    static binary from the releases page.
- Distribution: one static binary, ~12MB (the site's "10+MB"), no runtime
  dependencies. macOS / Linux / Windows, amd64 and arm64. UPX compresses a build to
  roughly a third — measured: Windows v0.2.7 11.8MB -> 3.4MB (the site's "5MB 以内"),
  dev Linux 15.4MB -> 4.7MB. UPX support for signed macOS arm64 binaries is not
  guaranteed.
- Remote hosts need only SSH. Credentials live in the local Termcp instance and are
  never handed to the model. Nothing of Termcp runs on the target.
- Extensions (`kind` = `mcp` | `skill` | `prompt` | `custom`) are pinned,
  capability-trimmed sessions kept warm and restarted automatically:
  - `mcp`: a stdio MCP server (`command` + `args`) or an HTTP/SSE endpoint (`url`).
  - `skill`: a read-only window onto remote files, scoped by a `paths` whitelist.
  - `prompt`: an interactive terminal with operating instructions attached.
  - `target` is a profile name (see "ssh_config" below), or `internal` for loopback.
    The same template with a different `target` is the same MCP on another machine.
- Extensions that dial the same host with the same whitelist share one connection,
  each driving its own shell channel.

## `cmd` is a shell-like DSL — NOT a shell

This is the single thing most callers get wrong.

- `cmd` holds DIRECTIVES only. A shell command enters as a VALUE — through `args`
  (`$1`, `$2`, … `${10}`) or `vars` (`$NAME`) — never as syntax.
- `&&`, `||`, `;` and `&` are DIRECTIVE separators, parsed by Termcp:
  - `;` — run the next statement regardless
  - `&&` — run the next statement only if this one answered 2xx
  - `||` — run the next statement only if this one did NOT answer 2xx
  - `&` — run this statement in PARALLEL: it does not wait for the statements
    around it. The reply still lists every slot in the order you wrote them, each
    with its own byte cursor (`Content-Range`). `&` is not "background job output
    you will read later".
  - A skipped statement still appears in the reply, as a slot with 208.
- `|`, `>`, `>>` and `<` are NOT Termcp operators. Inside a `run`/`type` payload
  they belong to the shell, because that payload IS a shell line.
- Two spellings of the same intent, and only one of them is what you want:

  ```
  run a1f3:1 $1     args: ["make && test"]     one shell line (the && is the shell's)
  run a1f3:1 make && notify done               two cmd statements (the && is Termcp's)
  ```

- Positional values (`args`):
  - A `$N` that IS the whole payload of `run`/`type` is spliced VERBATIM: that is
    how `pwd; whoami` reaches the terminal as two commands.
  - A `$N` anywhere else (beside other words, in a flag value, in a target) is
    substituted as ONE QUOTED WORD, so a value can never turn into syntax you did
    not write.
  - `vars` values are ALWAYS one quoted word: `vars` is the data channel.
  - `$0` is refused; `${N}` is the unambiguous spelling for N >= 10.
- Expansions Termcp does not own — `$$`, `$?`, `$@`, `$(…)`, `${x:-y}` — are left
  untouched for the shell to expand.
- A `cmd` is parsed IN FULL before any of it runs. One bad statement means nothing
  executes:
  `nothing was executed, including the N statement(s) before this one: a cmd is
  parsed in full before any of it runs`. An unknown directive is a 400
  `unknown_directive` — same rule, nothing ran.
- Values are tokenized before parsing, so a `&&` inside `args[0]` can never be
  mistaken for a Termcp operator.
- Known build difference: on some builds a `$N` immediately followed by `&` or `;`
  is substituted QUOTED (a bug, fixed on dev). If a command line seems to arrive as
  one word — the `Path:` echo shows quotes — write the command literally in `cmd`
  instead of through `args`.

## The command surface belongs to the RUNNING instance

Do not carry a spelling in from memory or from an older document. Ask the instance:

- `term` with an empty `cmd` returns the guide (where am I, what can I do),
- `help` returns the directive table,
- `help <verb>` documents that verb.

The surface has been renamed between releases, and the old names are gone
(`unknown_directive`, nothing executed):

| older | current |
|---|---|
| `ps` | `ls` |
| `host list` | `ls host` |
| `ext list` | `ls ext` |
| `fwd --action list` | `ls <session> forward` |

There is no `ext` directive and no `help ext`. The extension layer is reached
through the shared verbs: `ls ext`, `create ext <name> --kind mcp …`,
`edit ext <name>`, `rm ext <name>`.

As of v0.2.8-rc.4 the surface is:

```
connect <host> [--argv <command>] [--on-exit keep|close] [--name …]
open <session> [--argv <cmd> [--pty]] | open <session> forward …
ls | ls host | ls ext | ls alias | ls <session> [forward|file]
get <session|channel|host-name> | get <session> file <path> …
run <session> <index> <line>      input <session> <index> <text>
read <session> <index> …          write <session> file <path> …
create host|ext|alias <name> [flags]      edit host|ext|alias <name> [flags]
rm <session> | rm <session> file <path> | rm host|ext|alias <name>
notify [--level …] [--sticky] [--on <session>] [--title T] <body>
help [verb]
```

An address is `<session>:<index>` (`a1f3:1`). Take it from `ls` and copy it; never
spell one from memory.

## "ssh_config" is Termcp's own store

It is NOT OpenSSH's `~/.ssh/config`, and it is not read from there. It is Termcp's
own connection profile store (`ssh_configs/`, TOML records) holding `host`, `user`,
`password`, `private_key`, `key_passphrase`, `port`, `proxy`/jump, `known_hosts`,
`default_shell`, `default_mode` and `default_approval`. `internal` is a built-in
loopback profile. The name is borrowed; the content is not OpenSSH's.

Writing host profiles requires the instance to be started with
`--mcp-manage-ssh-configs`. Without it the call is refused with 403, and no call can
turn the switch on.

## Where a remote MCP actually runs

- `command` + `args`: the program runs ON the target, over SSH. It has to exist
  there (e.g. `npx -y …`). Termcp itself is not installed on the target.
- `url` (HTTP/SSE endpoint): the relay runs INSIDE termcp, so reaching a remote MCP
  server needs no second binary and no PATH lookup on the target.

## Boundaries — read before driving Termcp

- A call outside an extension's whitelist (`allow` / `paths`) is refused with a
  `forbidden` error. It is not transient: do not retry it and do not look for a way
  around it. If you need the capability, say so to the user.
- Review mode is per session and is configured by the user (a profile's
  `default_approval`, or the console's review switch). When it is on, creating or
  updating an extension — and writes it gates — returns HTTP 202: wait for the human
  rather than retrying.
- Extension sessions are kept OUT of the session list: `ls` does not show them,
  `ls ext` does. The reconciler keeps them warm and reports their state, so read the
  handle from `ls ext` when you need one instead of holding an old one.
- Extensions on the same host with the same whitelist share one connection (see
  Facts), so closing or deleting a session by hand can take down more than the thing
  you meant to close. Leave the sessions that `ls ext` names alone.
- Secrets (sudo passwords, MFA prompts, `[Y/n]` questions) are handed back to the
  human and stay inside the shell; they do not enter the model context.

## About termcp.org (the human-facing page)

- The terminal on that page is a SCRIPTED REPLAY. It calls no model and no server;
  typing into it does not reach a real shell. Do not treat it as an endpoint.
- Its examples use the current spelling (`ls host`, `connect node-1`,
  `run a1f3:1 $1`, `open a1f3 forward …`), matching the table above.
- Its size claims map to the figures in Facts: "single file 10+MB" is the ~12MB
  binary, "UPX 5MB 以内" is the compressed build.
- The Docker command shown there uses `--disable-auth` AND binds the port to
  `127.0.0.1`. That pairing is the only reason it is safe; it is not a general
  posture to copy onto a reachable interface.
- The credits list humans and one AI maintainer (the agent that wrote the site). An
  AI can be a maintainer or a contributor; it cannot donate.
